articles.title: Claude Code skill arguments across 12 runs: what $ARGUMENTS, $0 and argument-hint actually put in the body
articles.excerpt: Across 12 claude -p runs on Claude Code 2.1.278, $ARGUMENTS always carried the raw string exactly as typed (quotes included), $0/$1/$2 were split shell-style with quotes stripped, a missing positional…
articles.body: Across 12 claude -p runs on Claude Code 2.1.278, $ARGUMENTS always carried the raw string exactly as typed (quotes included), $0 / $1 / $2 were split shell-style with quotes stripped, a missing positional stayed as the literal text $2 , and argument-hint changed nothing in what the skill body received. One surprise: a bare $HOME or $ARGUMENTS token typed as an argument vanished from the positional slots while surviving in $ARGUMENTS . We run a small shop on Claude Code and most of our repeatable work lives in skills that get invoked as slash commands with arguments. When a skill misbehaves, the first question is always the same: what did the body actually receive after substitution?

articles.title: Before You Push: Building a Local Twin for GitHub Actions
articles.excerpt: Before You Push: Building a Local Twin for GitHub Actions There is a particular kind of frustration every developer eventually learns. You write the workflow. You read it twice. You check the indentat…
articles.body: Before You Push: Building a Local Twin for GitHub Actions There is a particular kind of frustration every developer eventually learns. You write the workflow. You read it twice. You check the indentation. You push. And then GitHub tells you that something was wrong all along. Maybe an environment variable was missing. Maybe an action was pinned incorrectly. Maybe two jobs were never connected the way you thought they were. Maybe a command worked perfectly on your machine and failed somewhere else. And suddenly, the feedback loop becomes: write ↓ push ↓ wait ↓ fail ↓ read logs ↓ change something ↓ push again I wanted a different loop. Not a fake GitHub Actions emulator that simply says everything is fine. Something more honest.

articles.title: Stop Healing Your Tests: Why Throwaway Automation Fits the AI Era
articles.excerpt: Self-healing tests are solving the wrong problem. When a "healer" swaps a broken locator for a "close enough" element, the run stays green, but the test might now be asserting something nobody intende…
articles.body: Self-healing tests are solving the wrong problem. When a "healer" swaps a broken locator for a "close enough" element, the run stays green, but the test might now be asserting something nobody intended. You haven't fixed the test. You've traded a loud failure for a quiet false positive. Here's the alternative I keep coming back to: don't maintain a script at all. If a model can read a test case and execute it in a browser by itself, the script stops being the thing you need. The test case is. You can't break a script that doesn't exist. Self-healing fixes the symptom A self-healing locator answers "the button moved, how do I still click it?" It never asks "should this script still exist?" Worse, a healer can swap a broken selector for a nearby element that looks plausible.

articles.title: I Ran My Career Like a Production System for 12 Weeks. The Dashboard Was Wrong Before I Was.
articles.excerpt: For 25 years I've been the person in the room asking to see the data. In incident reviews, in planning meetings, in one-on-ones with engineers who were sure their service was fine because nobody had c…
articles.body: For 25 years I've been the person in the room asking to see the data. In incident reviews, in planning meetings, in one-on-ones with engineers who were sure their service was fine because nobody had complained yet, I've said some version of the same sentence: if you can't see it, you can't run it. I believed it. I still do. But this summer I noticed something that made me more curious than I expected: I had spent a whole career measuring other people's work and had never once measured my own. My own career ran on good intentions: learn more about agents, write more, finally ship something. All true, all vague, and all impossible to learn from, because you can't miss a target you never set. And if you can't miss, you can't find out anything new.

The 2010s were certainly a better decade for the superhero sub-genre of sci-fi than the 2020s have been, particularly for Marvel Studios, but there have still been some breakout comic book films like Deadpool & Wolverine , Superman , and Spider-Man movie that broke every box office record in Hollywood history. articles.body: Diablo 4 director Brent Gibson is telling fans not to worry about the game after Diablo 5’s announcement sparked concerns about the former title’s lifespan. Diablo 5’s reveal at Blizzcon 2026 left fans equal parts excited and worried. Of course, players were pumped for a new Diablo game — but with Diablo 4 having just launched in 2023, the reveal of a new game so soon felt like a death knell for the one they were still playing. But Brent Gibson, director of Diablo 4, says there’s nothing to fuss about. Speaking with Icy Veins , Gibson outlined some plans for the game’s future content, saying it will continue to receive support well after 5’s release. “I have an analogy,” he began. “If you’re wearing a sign in the middle of Times Square saying, ‘The end is nigh,’ the end is not nigh.

articles.body: David Jaffe, the creator, co-writer, and director for the original God of War game, has cleared up his viral comments about Ariel Lawrence, creative director for Laufey. Ariel Lawrence has been with the God of War franchise since its very first game — but creator David Jaffe, who left the series behind in 2007 to form his own studio, says he never got along with her during his time at Santa Monica Studio. He described their contentious work relationship in a September 2026 live stream while reacting to footage for God of War Laufey , where he claimed their personalities clashed and that he didn’t feel as though she was truly passionate about the games they were making. “I have no problem with female directors at all,” he began.

articles.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Sol with Astra-like performance on a budget
articles.excerpt: Access gets started with ChatGPT Work and Codex, but Chat will have to wait.
articles.body: TL;DR OpenAI is introducing GPT-6.1 Sol, promising Astra-like performance at one-fifth the expenditure. Across numerous benchmarks, GPT-6.1 Sol comes close to 6 Astra’s capabilities, and outpaces GPT-6 Sol. GPT-6.1 demonstrates fewer factual errors than GPT-6 Sol across similar tests. DevDay is here for OpenAI, and that means the company is sharing a whole bunch of news about its latest work on models and the services built around them. While we just heard that GPT-6.1 Astra is getting sent back to the bench for misbehaving, progress continues on the rest of OpenAI’s headlining models, and this afternoon we’re getting the scoop on the first member of that 6.1-series to actually make its public debut, with the launch of GPT‑6.1 Sol.
